# Part C — Decision memo

*Envelope generated by `make partc` from `ablation, adversarial, analysis, bench, corpus_stats, partc, sample_manifest`.
Commit `fd3e481e89b59415a68867936ab60e0d233b0818-dirty`.*

Paths on the table: **(a)** SFT on synthetic "casualized" pairs, **(b)** a
small inference-time rewriter after the main model, **(c)** prompt engineering
only.

## Assumptions

Stated constraints: 1× A100-80GB for 2 weeks;
1 native-speaker reviewer covering
2 of 6 target languages
at 10 h/week; review launches in
3 weeks; no external API budget.

Estimates I am supplying, each challengeable: reviewer throughput
80 items/h; 15000 SFT pairs;
4 sentences per response;
3 epochs; LoRA throughput between
3000 and 6000 tokens/s.

**No external API budget** means synthetic pairs cannot come from a frontier
API; they must be generated by our own model on the same A100 that trains it.

## Arithmetic

### Human evaluation capacity

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| reviewer-hours over the project | 20 |
| items at the stated rate | 1600 |
| items per covered language | 800 |
| items per language if split evenly across all targets | 266 |
| languages with zero native-speaker coverage | 4 |

Uncovered: ben, mar, tam, tel.

### Training cost

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| measured tokens per response (Indic mean, Indic-aware tokenizer) | 119.0 |
| training tokens (15000 pairs × 3 epochs) | 5355089 |
| GPU-hours at the higher throughput estimate | 0.25 |
| GPU-hours at the lower throughput estimate | 0.50 |
| GPU-hours available | 336 |
| utilisation at the lower estimate | 0.00148 |

Sensitivity — GPU-hours at the lower throughput estimate, by dataset size:
5000 pairs → 0.17 h; 15000 pairs → 0.50 h; 50000 pairs → 1.65 h.

### Serving cost of path (b)

Measured output goodput is 200.92 tok/s (B3, batch
24). A rewriter regenerates the whole response, so it adds a
second pass over the same output-token count: 100.46 tok/s
if the rewriter costs the same per token, on the same hardware and batch.

## Recommendation

**Path (a): a LoRA SFT pass on synthetic casualized pairs, with path (c) built
first as the day-one control and the fallback.**

Not (b). A rewriter regenerates the whole response, so it adds a second pass
over the same output tokens: measured goodput falls from 200.92 to
100.46 tok/s on the same hardware and batch. That is a
permanent serving tax on every request, in every language, paid for a change of
register.

Not (c) alone. Prompt engineering consumes context on every request forever and
does not persist across model updates. It is the right control and the right
fallback, and it is not a durable answer.

(a), because the arithmetic below says its cost is negligible and its risk is
concentrated in one assumption that day one can test.

## Success metric

**On a held-out set of 400 items per reviewed
language (800 of the 1600-item
budget), at least 60 % of SFT responses rated
4 or better for casual register on a
5-point scale, against a prompt-engineered baseline.**

The threshold is set against reviewer capacity, not against ambition: at
80 items/hour the reviewer can score that volume inside
the 20 available hours and still leave budget for the
pilot below. The reviewer is used as an **evaluator scoring model output**, not
as a labeller producing training data — 1600 items is far
too few to train on and ample to judge with.

## Kill criterion

**By 2026-09-21: if a 200-item pilot
shows SFT winning fewer than 55 % of head-to-head
comparisons against the prompt-engineered baseline in Hindi and Kannada,
abandon (a) and ship (c).**

That date is the GPU budget's exhaustion and one week before review launch on
2026-09-28 — the last point at which falling back to (c) still
leaves time to validate it.

## Day-1 experiment

**On 2026-09-08: generate 200 casualized Hindi
pairs with our own model, and have the reviewer score
100 of the synthetic *targets* — not model output, the
training data itself — for whether they are acceptable casual Hindi.**

With no external API budget the pairs must come off our own model on the same
A100. The entire SFT path therefore rests on one assumption: that the model can
already produce the register we want to train it to produce, just not
reliably. If it cannot, SFT would be distilling our own formality back into
itself, and no amount of GPU time fixes that. This is the cheapest possible
test of the load-bearing assumption, and a negative result kills (a) on day one
before any training run.

## The constraint that decides this

**Human evaluation, and language coverage within it. The GPU is not close to
binding.**

Training needs 0.50 GPU-hours of the
336 available — 0.15 % of
the allocation. At 50000 pairs it is still under
1.7 hours. Any plan that spends its planning
effort on training throughput is optimising a term that rounds to nothing.

The binding terms are that one reviewer produces 1600
scored items in total, and that 4 of the
6 target languages —
ben, mar, tam, tel — have **no native speaker at all**.

Design around it rather than through it: ship to Hindi and Kannada first, where
the claim is evidenced. For the other 4, calibrate an
automatic proxy — a formality classifier or perplexity shift — against the
human scores on Hindi and Kannada, and use it as a **regression gate, not as
evidence of quality**. Those four languages ship on an assumption of transfer,
and that assumption should be stated in the launch decision rather than
absorbed into an aggregate number.
